deepDives.title: Generating unique codes
deepDives.body: Take a globally increasing number and encode it in base62 (a–z, A–Z, 0–9): 7 characters give 62^7 ≈ 3.5 trillion codes. To avoid one counter becoming a bottleneck, each write server grabs a batch of, say, 1,000 IDs at a time from a central counter (Redis INCRBY or a database sequence) and hands them out locally. Hashing the long URL also works but needs collision checks and retries; random codes are harder to guess, which some products want.

deepDives.title: Fast, highly available redirects
deepDives.body: Redirects dominate traffic, so put an in-memory cache (Redis) in front of the database and let a CDN cache popular redirects at the edge. Use 302 if you want every click to reach you (analytics, editable destinations); 301 lets browsers cache the redirect and cuts load but loses visibility.

deepDives.title: Custom aliases and expiry
deepDives.body: A custom alias is just a chosen short_code: insert it with a uniqueness check (the primary key rejects duplicates). Keep generated codes and aliases in the same table so they can't collide. Store expires_at, check it on redirect, and remove expired rows with a background job or database TTL.

deepDives.title: Scaling storage
deepDives.body: A billion links of ~500 bytes is ~500 GB, which fits a small cluster. If it grows, partition by short_code hash so reads spread evenly.

deepDives.title: Uploading large files
deepDives.body: The client splits files into chunks (e.g. 5–10 MB), hashes each one, and asks the file service which chunks are missing. It uploads those in parallel straight to object storage with pre-signed URLs (S3 multipart upload), retrying individual parts. When all parts are in, the metadata status flips to uploaded, either confirmed by the client or by storage events.

deepDives.title: Deduplication and delta sync
deepDives.body: Because chunks are named by content hash, an edited file only re-uploads the chunks that changed, and identical chunks across files or users are stored once.

deepDives.title: Keeping devices in sync
deepDives.body: Every change appends to the user's change log with an increasing cursor. Clients remember their last cursor and ask for newer changes, via long polling or a WebSocket nudge, then download what changed. Local changes go through the same upload path.

deepDives.title: Conflicts
deepDives.body: If two devices edit the same version offline, keep both: save the later one as a conflict copy (or a new version) rather than silently overwriting. Version numbers on the metadata row detect the conflict (optimistic concurrency).

Enforce one review per user per business with a unique constraint
Keep the search index in sync with the database (change data capture or events)
Paginate search results and reviews (cursor-based)
Cache popular searches and business pages; the workload is read-heavy

deepDives.title: Proximity search
deepDives.body: Index each business's location in a geospatial index: Elasticsearch geo_point with a geo_distance filter, PostGIS, or geohash prefixes. Businesses rarely move, so updates are cheap. Combine the location filter with text and category matching, then rank by distance, rating and relevance.

deepDives.title: Average ratings
deepDives.body: Store avg_rating and review_count on the business row. When a review is added, update both atomically in the same transaction as the insert (new_avg = (avg × count + rating) / (count + 1)), so concurrent reviews don't overwrite each other.

deepDives.title: One review per user
deepDives.body: A unique constraint on (business_id, user_id) enforces it at the database, not just in the UI.

deepDives.title: Keeping search in sync
deepDives.body: The relational database is the source of truth. Change data capture publishes changes to the search index within seconds; slight delay is acceptable for search.

Prevent overselling: decrement stock atomically in a transaction when an order is placed
Cache availability for browsing (read-heavy) with a short TTL
Partition data by region or distribution centre

Orders and payments are idempotent and tracked through statuses

deepDives.title: Which centres can serve a customer
deepDives.body: Pre-filter centres within a radius using a geospatial index, then confirm with travel times (a maps/ETA service) for the few candidates. Cache the centre list per area, since centres don't move.

deepDives.title: Preventing overselling
deepDives.body: Placing an order runs one transaction: lock or conditionally update each inventory row (UPDATE … SET qty = qty − n WHERE qty ≥ n), and fail the whole order if any item is short. Take payment with an idempotency key; if payment fails, release the stock.

deepDives.title: Fast availability at scale
deepDives.body: Availability reads far outnumber orders. Serve them from read replicas and a short-TTL cache per area; a few seconds of staleness is fine because the order transaction is the final check.

rubric.point: Reserve a seat with a temporary hold that expires (e.g. 10 minutes) so a buyer can pay without someone else grabbing it
Never double-book: the final booking is a conditional write or transaction that only succeeds if the seat is still available
Keep holds in Redis with a TTL (or a status + expires_at column) so abandoned checkouts free the seat automatically
Put a virtual waiting room in front of hot events so only a controlled number of users reach seat selection at once
Search events by keyword, date, venue and location with a search index (Elasticsearch) fed by change data capture
Show a live seat map: push seat status changes to viewers over SSE or WebSockets instead of letting them hit a taken seat
Payments go through a provider (e.g. Stripe) with an idempotency key; the booking is confirmed only on a successful payment webhook
Cache event and venue details (and search results) heavily, since they change rarely and are read by millions
Separate the read-heavy browse/search path from the strongly consistent booking path, scaling each independently
Numbers: a big on-sale can bring millions of users for tens of thousands of seats within minutes

Browse/search and booking run as separate services and scale independently

deepDives.title: Holding seats without double booking
deepDives.body: When a user picks seats, write a hold in Redis with SET seat_id user_id NX EX 600, so only one user gets it and it expires on its own after 10 minutes if they walk away. The confirm step then runs a database transaction that moves each ticket from available to booked only if its status and version still match (optimistic concurrency), so even a Redis failure can't cause a double booking. An alternative is to keep status = held plus hold_expires_at in the database and treat expired holds as available; this avoids a second system but needs a cleanup job and more database load.

deepDives.title: Surviving the on-sale spike
deepDives.body: For a big on-sale, put users into a virtual waiting room before they reach the seat map. A queue (e.g. a Redis sorted set by arrival time) tracks positions, and an admission worker lets in a few thousand at a time as others finish or their holds expire. Users see their queue position over a WebSocket or SSE connection. This protects the booking database and gives a fairer experience than letting everyone race and fail.

deepDives.title: Fast event search
deepDives.body: A SQL LIKE query over millions of events is slow, so index events in Elasticsearch with full-text fields for names and performers, plus geo and date filters. Keep it in sync with CDC from the primary database; a few seconds of lag is fine. Cache popular queries and put event pages behind a CDN, since they rarely change.

deepDives.title: Live seat map
deepDives.body: Polling the seat map for thousands of viewers is wasteful and stale. Instead the booking service publishes seat status changes, and viewers connected over SSE receive them in real time, so held and booked seats grey out immediately. For the hottest events it can be simpler to show section-level availability and auto-assign the best seats.

deepDives.title: Payments
deepDives.body: Send the payment to a provider with an idempotency key tied to the booking, so retries never charge twice. Confirm the booking when the provider's webhook reports success; if payment fails or the hold expires first, release the seats.

Serve media from a CDN, and generate thumbnails / multiple resolutions (and video transcoding) asynchronously after upload
Build the feed with fan-out on write: when someone posts, push the post ID into each follower's precomputed feed
Handle celebrities with a hybrid: don't fan out for accounts with millions of followers; merge their posts in at read time
Store precomputed feeds in Redis as a capped list/sorted set of post IDs per user, then hydrate post details
Model the follow graph for both directions (followers and following) in a table partitioned by user, e.g. DynamoDB / Cassandra
Paginate the feed with a cursor (last post ID / timestamp) rather than offsets
Fan-out runs asynchronously through a message queue and workers so posting stays fast
Accept eventual consistency: a new post may take a few seconds to reach followers' feeds

Users follow other users

deepDives.title: Fan-out on write vs read
deepDives.body: Computing a feed at read time means querying hundreds of followed accounts and merging, which is too slow at this scale. Instead, fan out on write: when a post is created, workers push its ID into a Redis sorted set for each follower, capped at a few hundred entries. Reads become a single cache lookup followed by hydrating post details. The cost is write amplification and a delay of a few seconds, which is acceptable.

deepDives.title: Celebrities
deepDives.body: Fanning out a post to 100 million followers is too expensive and slow. Use a hybrid: accounts above a follower threshold are skipped by fan-out, and at read time the feed service pulls their recent posts (cached, since everyone reads them) and merges them with the precomputed feed by timestamp. Inactive users can also be skipped and have their feed rebuilt on their next visit.

deepDives.title: Media upload and delivery
deepDives.body: Large files shouldn't pass through app servers. The client asks for pre-signed S3 URLs, uploads directly (multipart and resumable for videos), and S3 notifies a pipeline that creates thumbnails, several resolutions and adaptive video renditions. The post becomes visible once processing finishes, and all media is served from a CDN close to the viewer.

deepDives.title: Pagination and storage
deepDives.body: Feeds are paginated with a cursor (the timestamp or ID of the last post seen) so new posts at the top don't shift pages. Posts are partitioned by author and the follow table has an index keyed each way, so 'who follows X' and 'who does X follow' are both single-partition queries.

rubric.point: Precompute each user's feed with fan-out on write: a new post's ID is pushed to every friend's/follower's feed
Avoid the hot-key problem for users/pages with millions of followers: skip fan-out for them and pull their posts at read time (hybrid)
Keep the precomputed feed as a capped list of post IDs in a cache (Redis), then hydrate the full posts from a post cache
Run fan-out asynchronously: publish post events to Kafka/a queue and let a pool of workers write to followers' feeds
Store the social graph efficiently so 'who follows X' is one lookup, e.g. a follow table with an index in both directions
Paginate with a cursor based on timestamp or post ID so infinite scroll stays stable as new posts arrive
Cache hot posts: a viral post is read by millions, so replicate it across cache nodes or keep it in a local in-process cache
Rank or order posts: start chronological, optionally rank by affinity, engagement and recency in a separate ranking step
Accept eventual consistency: a post can take a few seconds to appear in friends' feeds, in exchange for availability
Numbers: ~2 billion users, unbounded follows, feed reads must return in under ~500 ms

deepDives.title: Why precompute feeds
deepDives.body: A naive feed query gathers posts from every followed user and sorts them, which is slow when someone follows thousands of accounts. Fan-out on write moves that work to post time: workers push the new post ID into each follower's feed list, capped at around 500 entries. Reads then become a single cache lookup plus hydration, which comfortably meets the latency target. Feeds for users who haven't logged in for a while can be dropped and rebuilt on demand.

deepDives.title: High-follower accounts
deepDives.body: A page with 50 million followers would create 50 million writes per post, delaying everyone's feed. Mark such accounts and skip fan-out for them; at read time the feed service fetches their recent posts (which are heavily cached) and merges them with the precomputed list. This hybrid keeps write amplification bounded while reads stay fast.

deepDives.title: Hot posts
deepDives.body: A viral post is requested by millions of feeds at once, which can overload the single cache shard holding it. Replicate hot post entries across several cache nodes and pick one at random, or keep them in a short-lived local in-process cache on each feed server. Like and comment counts can be updated asynchronously and shown slightly stale.

deepDives.title: Ordering and pagination
deepDives.body: Start with reverse-chronological order, which the sorted feed list gives for free. Pagination uses a cursor (the timestamp or ID of the last post returned) so new posts arriving at the top don't cause duplicates. A ranking step can later rescore candidates by affinity, engagement and recency before returning a page.

Record swipes at high write volume in a write-optimised, partitioned store (e.g. Cassandra) keyed by swiper
Detect a match atomically: when A likes B, check if B already liked A in one consistent operation so no match is missed when both swipe at once
Use a fast store like Redis for pending likes so the 'did they like me back?' check is instant
Notify both users of a match immediately with a push notification (APNs/FCM)
Precompute and cache each user's stack of recommendations so opening the app is instant, refreshing it in the background
Don't show profiles a user already swiped on: filter with a per-user seen set, or a bloom filter for large histories
Update locations sparingly: clients send location only when they move significantly, and the geo index is updated asynchronously
Numbers: tens of millions of daily users making billions of swipes per day, i.e. tens of thousands of writes per second

deepDives.title: Never missing a match
deepDives.body: If A and B swipe right on each other at the same instant, two separate 'write my like, then check theirs' steps can both miss. Make the check atomic: keep likes in Redis keyed by the sorted pair (min_id:max_id) and use a Lua script that records this side's like and reads the other side's in one step, so whichever arrives second always sees the match. Swipes are also written durably to Cassandra; a periodic job can reconcile if Redis loses data.

deepDives.title: Finding nearby candidates fast
deepDives.body: Scanning all users by distance is far too slow. Index locations with a geospatial index (Elasticsearch geo queries, PostGIS, or geohash cells) and combine them with preference filters. To keep the index manageable, clients only send a location update when the user has moved significantly, and updates are applied asynchronously; a few minutes of staleness is fine.

deepDives.title: Instant stacks
deepDives.body: Rather than running the geo query on every app open, precompute a stack of, say, 200 candidates per active user and cache it. When the client is near the end of its deck, it fetches more while a background job refreshes the stack. Stacks carry a short TTL so users who travel get fresh results.

deepDives.title: Avoiding repeat profiles
deepDives.body: Filter out anyone the user already swiped on. For most users a set of seen IDs works; for heavy users with long histories, a per-user bloom filter keeps memory small, at the cost of occasionally hiding a profile they never saw (false positives), which is harmless.

Enforce CPU time, memory and wall-clock limits per run, killing submissions that exceed them (and seccomp to block dangerous system calls)
Decouple submission from execution: put submissions on a queue and let a pool of workers pull and run them
Autoscale the worker pool (and keep warm containers per language) to absorb contest spikes
Return results by having the client poll a submission status endpoint (or a WebSocket/SSE push) until the verdict is ready
Keep a live contest leaderboard in a Redis sorted set updated on each accepted submission, ranked by score then time/penalty
Serve the leaderboard cheaply: clients poll every few seconds and the top pages are cached rather than recomputed per viewer
Store test cases in object storage and load them into the runner; each test's output is compared with the expected output
Numbers: most of the year traffic is modest, but a contest brings ~100k users submitting within a 90-minute window

deepDives.title: Running untrusted code safely
deepDives.body: Every submission runs in a fresh, isolated sandbox: a container with gVisor or a Firecracker microVM, one image per language. The sandbox has no network access, a read-only filesystem apart from a scratch directory, a non-root user, and seccomp filters on system calls. cgroups enforce CPU time and memory limits, and a watchdog kills anything that exceeds the time limit, returning 'Time Limit Exceeded'.

deepDives.title: Absorbing contest spikes
deepDives.body: Submissions go onto a queue so a burst never overloads the runners; the queue simply grows and drains. Worker pools autoscale on queue depth, and keeping pre-warmed containers for popular languages avoids cold-start delays. Because contests are scheduled, capacity can also be scaled up ahead of the start time.

deepDives.title: Getting the verdict back
deepDives.body: Execution takes a few seconds, so the submit call returns a submission ID immediately. The client polls a status endpoint once a second, which is simple and cheap at this scale; a WebSocket or SSE push works too but adds connection management for little gain.

deepDives.title: Live leaderboard
deepDives.body: Querying and sorting all submissions for every viewer would crush the database. Instead, on each accepted submission update a Redis sorted set per contest with ZADD, encoding score and penalty time into one number so the order is correct. Reading a page is a ZREVRANGE; clients poll every few seconds and the top page is cached briefly. The database remains the source of truth, so the sorted set can be rebuilt if lost.

deepDives.title: Routing between chat servers
deepDives.body: With hundreds of millions of connections spread over thousands of servers, the sender and recipient are usually on different machines. Each chat server subscribes to a Redis pub/sub channel for every user connected to it; to deliver, the sender's server publishes to the recipient's channel. Pub/sub is fire-and-forget, which is fine because the durable copy is already in the database and inbox. An alternative is a connection registry (user → server) with direct server-to-server calls, which needs care when users reconnect elsewhere.

deepDives.title: Never losing a message
deepDives.body: A message is written to the database and to each recipient's inbox before the sender gets an ack. The recipient's client acknowledges receipt, and only then is the inbox entry removed; unacked messages are resent on reconnect. This is at-least-once delivery, so every message carries a client-generated ID and clients drop duplicates, making retries idempotent.

deepDives.title: Offline users and multiple devices
deepDives.body: When a user is offline, messages accumulate in their inbox and a push notification is sent via APNs/FCM. On reconnect, the client fetches everything in the inbox since its last sync. For multiple devices, keep an inbox per device (or per-device sync cursors) so each device gets every message once.

deepDives.title: Group chats
deepDives.body: A group message is stored once and fanned out to each member: an inbox entry plus a pub/sub publish per member. Capping groups at a few hundred members bounds the write amplification; very large broadcast channels would need a pull model instead.

Upload activities asynchronously: store the raw GPS track (or GPX/FIT file) in object storage and process it in the background via a queue

Leaderboards (per segment or among friends) kept in Redis sorted sets, updated as activities are processed
Activity feed of friends' workouts, built from the follow graph (fan-out or query-on-read, since volumes are modest)
Partition activities by user so a user's history is one fast range query
Numbers: ~10 million daily activities, a few seconds per GPS sample, a 1-hour run is a few thousand points

deepDives.title: Recording offline and on battery
deepDives.body: GPS works without a signal, so the device records points locally every few seconds and computes distance (haversine between consecutive points), pace and elapsed time itself. It uploads in batches when connected, and the full track on completion, which saves battery and data. Uploads carry the activity ID and point timestamps so retries are idempotent and no activity is lost.

deepDives.title: Storing routes
deepDives.body: A one-hour run at one sample every two seconds is ~1,800 points; one row per point across millions of activities is wasteful. Keep the raw track as a compressed file in object storage for reprocessing, and store an encoded, downsampled polyline on the activity record for drawing maps. Summary stats are precomputed so history pages never touch raw points.

deepDives.title: Live sharing
deepDives.body: During an activity with sharing on, the device sends its latest location every 5–10 seconds. Followers watching poll for the latest point, or receive it over SSE/WebSocket; since updates are infrequent and viewers few, polling is usually enough. The latest location is kept in Redis with a short TTL.

deepDives.title: Leaderboards
deepDives.body: When processing matches an activity to a popular segment, the effort time is added to that segment's Redis sorted set (ZADD with the time as score), giving an instant rank. Friend leaderboards can be computed on read by filtering the segment's efforts to the user's friends, since friend lists are small.

rubric.point: Spread keys across nodes with consistent hashing (a hash ring with virtual nodes) so adding or removing a node moves only a small share of keys
Evict when memory is full using LRU: a hash map plus a doubly linked list gives O(1) get, put and eviction
Support TTL expiry: lazily check expiry on read and run a periodic sweep to reclaim expired keys
Replicate each shard (primary with replicas, or to the next nodes on the ring) so a node failure doesn't lose the hot data
Detect failures and change membership with heartbeats/gossip or a coordinator (ZooKeeper/etcd), then promote a replica
Handle hot keys: replicate them to several nodes or add a small client-side local cache in front
Choose asynchronous replication and eventual consistency for speed, accepting a small window of stale or lost writes
Let clients route directly: they hold the ring/cluster map and hash keys themselves, avoiding an extra proxy hop
Numbers: ~1 TB of data across nodes with ~64 GB each, ~1 million operations per second, sub-millisecond to ~10 ms latency

deepDives.title: A single node: LRU and TTL
deepDives.body: Each node keeps a hash map from key to a node in a doubly linked list. A get moves the entry to the head, a put inserts at the head, and when memory is full the tail is evicted, all in O(1). Expiry is handled lazily (an expired key found on get is deleted and reported as a miss) plus a background sweep that samples keys and removes expired ones, so memory isn't wasted on keys nobody reads.

deepDives.title: Sharding with consistent hashing
deepDives.body: Modulo hashing (hash(key) % N) reshuffles almost every key when N changes, wiping out the cache. Consistent hashing places nodes on a hash ring and gives each key to the next node clockwise, so adding a node only moves the keys in its slice. Each physical node gets many virtual nodes so load stays even and a failed node's keys spread across many others.

deepDives.title: Availability and replication
deepDives.body: Each shard's primary replicates asynchronously to one or two replicas, which keeps writes fast; a failure may lose the last few writes, which is acceptable for a cache. Nodes send heartbeats, and when a primary goes quiet, a coordinator such as ZooKeeper or etcd (or a gossip protocol) promotes a replica and publishes the new cluster map. Replicas can also serve reads to add capacity, at the cost of slightly stale values.

deepDives.title: Hot keys and routing
deepDives.body: A single celebrity key can overload one node. Detect hot keys and copy them to several nodes (for example by appending a random suffix and reading any copy), or keep a tiny client-side local cache with a short TTL. Clients use a smart client library that caches the cluster map and routes directly to the owner node, avoiding an extra proxy hop; the map is refreshed when nodes change.

rubric.point: Pick and justify an algorithm: token bucket (allows bursts, smooth refill) vs fixed window (cheap but spiky at boundaries) vs sliding window log/counter (accurate, more memory)
Keep counters in a shared, fast store (Redis) so every gateway node sees the same limit, not per-node memory
Make check-and-update atomic: a Redis Lua script or INCR plus EXPIRE, so concurrent requests can't both slip under the limit
Place the limiter at the edge (API gateway or middleware) before requests reach backend services
Identify the client and configure rules: limits per API key, user ID or IP, per endpoint and tier, loaded from a config store
Reject cleanly: HTTP 429 Too Many Requests with Retry-After and X-RateLimit-Remaining headers
Decide what happens when Redis is down: fail open (allow traffic, protect availability) or fail closed (protect backends), with short timeouts
Cut round trips and hot keys: shard counters across a Redis cluster by client key, and batch or locally pre-allocate tokens for very busy clients
Keep the added latency tiny: one Redis call of about 1 ms per request, with Redis in the same region as the gateways
Multi-region or approximate limits: accept slightly loose global counts (sync regional counters asynchronously) rather than a cross-region call on every request

functional: Limit how many requests a client (API key, user or IP) can make to an endpoint in a time window

Clients over the limit get a clear rejection telling them when to retry

deepDives.title: Choosing an algorithm
deepDives.body: A fixed window counter (INCR a key per minute) is simplest but lets a client send double the limit across a window boundary. A sliding window log is exact but stores a timestamp per request, which is costly for big limits. A token bucket stores just two numbers per client, refills at a steady rate and allows controlled bursts, so it is a good default; a sliding window counter (weighted blend of two fixed windows) is a fine alternative when you think in requests per minute.

deepDives.title: Atomic updates in Redis
deepDives.body: Two gateway nodes reading a count, both seeing 99 of 100, and both writing 100 is a race condition that lets traffic through. Running the whole refill-check-decrement as one Lua script makes it atomic inside Redis and costs a single round trip. Keys get an expiry so idle clients' buckets disappear on their own.

deepDives.title: Failure handling and latency
deepDives.body: Redis is now on the hot path of every request, so calls use a tight timeout of a few milliseconds. If Redis is unreachable, most public APIs fail open (let requests through and log it) because rejecting all traffic is worse than briefly losing protection; a login or payment endpoint might fail closed instead. Replicas with automatic failover keep outages short.

deepDives.title: Hot keys and scale
deepDives.body: Sharding by client key across a Redis cluster spreads load, but one huge client can still make a hot key on a single shard. For those, a gateway can take a batch of tokens (say 100) at once and spend them from a local cache, trading a little accuracy for far fewer calls. Around 1 million requests per second is comfortably handled by a modest cluster when each check is one call.

deepDives.title: Multiple regions
deepDives.body: A strictly global limit would need a cross-region call per request, adding tens of milliseconds. Instead, each region enforces its own share or keeps local counters and syncs totals asynchronously, accepting approximate, slightly loose limits. This is usually fine because rate limits protect capacity rather than money.

rubric.point: Accept bids with a consistency guarantee: a new bid must beat the current highest, checked and written atomically (conditional update, optimistic concurrency or row lock)
Serialise bids per auction: route every bid for one auction to one partition or queue so they are processed in order
Never lose an accepted bid: persist it durably (write-ahead or queue) before acknowledging the bidder
Push live price updates to watchers over WebSockets or SSE, fanning out via pub/sub rather than having clients poll
End auctions exactly on time: a scheduler or delayed queue fires at end time, and bids arriving after the deadline are rejected by server timestamp
Handle the last-second bidding surge: the hottest auctions get the most bids just before closing, so the bid path must absorb spikes
Settle the winner idempotently: one close event picks the highest bid, notifies winner and seller, and starts payment exactly once
Keep an append-only bid history per auction as the source of truth, with the current max price as a derived, cached value
Optional: proxy (automatic) bidding, where the system bids for a user up to their maximum

deepDives.title: Accepting bids consistently
deepDives.body: Two people bidding £50 at the same moment must not both win. The simplest correct approach is an atomic conditional write: UPDATE auction SET current_max_bid = 50, version = v+1 WHERE id = ? AND current_max_bid < 50 AND version = v, retrying on conflict (optimistic concurrency). Under heavy contention this retries a lot, so for very hot auctions we route every bid for that auction through one partition and let a single writer apply them in order, which removes the race entirely.

deepDives.title: Durability and acknowledgements
deepDives.body: Bidders need to trust that 'bid accepted' means it counts. We persist the bid to a replicated log (Kafka with acks from all replicas) or the database before responding, so a crash never loses an accepted bid. The bid history is append-only, which doubles as an audit trail for disputes; current_max_bid is just a derived value we can rebuild.

deepDives.title: Real-time price updates
deepDives.body: Watchers hold a WebSocket (or SSE) connection to a stateless connection tier. After each accepted bid, the bid service publishes to the auction's pub/sub topic (Redis Pub/Sub or Kafka), and each connection server pushes to its local watchers. This fan out keeps updates under a second without millions of clients polling.

deepDives.title: Closing on time and last-second bids
deepDives.body: Each auction schedules a close event at its end time in a delayed queue or a time-bucketed scheduler table. Bids are timestamped by the server when they arrive, and anything after the deadline is rejected, so clock skew on clients doesn't matter. Many platforms counter sniping by extending the end time by a couple of minutes when a bid lands in the final minute. The surge right before closing is why the bid path must scale per auction, not just in total.

deepDives.title: Settlement and proxy bidding
deepDives.body: The close handler is idempotent: it marks the auction closed with a conditional update, so a retried event does nothing twice, then notifies the winner and seller and starts payment exactly once. Proxy bidding stores each user's hidden maximum bid; when outbid, the system automatically places the next increment for them up to that maximum, all inside the same serialised bid processing.

Transcode each upload into several resolutions and bitrates (e.g. 240p to 4K) and codecs so it plays on any device and network
Split the video into segments and transcode them in parallel on a worker fleet, orchestrated as a DAG of jobs via a queue
Stream with adaptive bitrate (HLS or DASH): short segments plus a manifest so the player switches quality as bandwidth changes
Serve video segments from a CDN close to viewers; the origin only handles cache misses
Keep video metadata (title, owner, status, available renditions) in a database separate from the video bytes in blob storage
Track processing status (uploading, processing, ready, failed) so the video only goes live when renditions exist, and retry failed jobs
Treat popularity unevenly: popular videos warm in CDN caches, while the long tail can stay in cheaper storage and fewer formats
Size it: hundreds of hours uploaded per minute and a huge read to write ratio, so the design is dominated by egress bandwidth and storage

deepDives.title: Uploading large files
deepDives.body: A 5 GB upload through app servers would tie them up for minutes. Instead the client requests pre-signed URLs and uploads chunks of about 10 MB directly to S3 with multipart upload; failed chunks are retried and an interrupted upload is resumed from the last completed part. When all parts land, the client (or a storage event) marks the upload complete and processing starts.

deepDives.title: Transcoding pipeline
deepDives.body: Raw uploads come in every format, so we transcode into a ladder of renditions such as 240p, 480p, 720p and 1080p at matching bitrates, in H.264 plus a newer codec for supported devices. Doing a 2-hour video on one machine is slow, so we split it into segments of a few seconds and fan them out as parallel jobs to a worker fleet via a queue. An orchestrator tracks this DAG (split, transcode, thumbnails, manifest), retries failed tasks and flips the status to ready only when the renditions exist.

deepDives.title: Adaptive bitrate streaming
deepDives.body: Each rendition is stored as short segments, and an HLS or DASH manifest lists them. The player measures its throughput and picks the best quality it can sustain, switching between segments as the network changes, which avoids buffering on a phone that moves from Wi-Fi to 4G. Short segments also make seeking cheap.

deepDives.title: Serving at scale with a CDN
deepDives.body: Almost all the cost is egress bandwidth. A CDN caches segments at edge locations near viewers, so popular videos are served without touching the origin. The long tail of rarely watched videos is fetched from origin on demand, and can move to cheaper storage tiers or keep fewer renditions to save money.

rubric.point: Separate job definitions (what and when, including cron expressions) from executions (one row per scheduled run with its own status)
Find due jobs efficiently: index executions by scheduled time and poll in small time buckets, rather than scanning all jobs
Use a two-stage design: a scheduler that enqueues due jobs into a message queue, and a separate pool of workers that execute them
Avoid double pick-up across scheduler instances: partition the time range, or claim rows with leases, locks or SELECT … FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
Guarantee at-least-once execution: workers heartbeat or hold a visibility timeout, and jobs whose worker died are re-queued
Because runs can repeat, jobs must be idempotent, e.g. using the execution ID as an idempotency key
Retry failures with exponential backoff and a max attempt count, then move them to a dead-letter queue
Recurring (cron) jobs: after each run, or ahead of time, compute and insert the next execution from the cron expression
Handle bursts and precision: jobs start within a second or so of their time even when many fire at midnight, by pre-loading upcoming jobs and scaling workers

Jobs are executed reliably at (or very shortly after) their scheduled time

nonFunctional: Jobs start within about 2 seconds of their scheduled time

deepDives.title: Finding due jobs quickly
deepDives.body: Scanning every job to see what's due does not scale. We keep an Execution row per scheduled run, indexed by scheduled_time, so a query for 'due in the next minute and still pending' reads a tiny slice. A common refinement is a two-level scheme: a database holds everything, and a poller loads the next few minutes into a Redis sorted set or a delayed queue (such as SQS delay) so that jobs fire with second-level precision.

deepDives.title: Avoiding double pick-up
deepDives.body: Several scheduler instances run for availability, so two of them must not enqueue the same execution. Each claims rows with a conditional update (status pending → queued) or SELECT … FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, or we partition the time buckets between instances with a leader or hash assignment. Even if a duplicate slips through, idempotent handling downstream makes it harmless.

deepDives.title: Reliable execution
deepDives.body: A worker takes a job with a visibility timeout or lease and sends heartbeats while it runs. If the worker crashes, the lease expires and the job is re-queued, giving at-least-once execution. Since a job can therefore run twice, tasks should be idempotent, for example passing the execution ID as an idempotency key to the downstream system. Failures are retried with exponential backoff up to a max attempts limit, then parked in a dead-letter queue for a human to inspect.

deepDives.title: Recurring jobs and bursts
deepDives.body: For a cron job, when an execution is created or completes, we compute the next occurrence and insert that execution too, so there is always one pending run ahead. Many users pick midnight or the top of the hour, creating bursts of thousands of jobs in the same second. Pre-loading upcoming jobs into the queue a little early, and autoscaling the worker pool on queue depth, keeps start delays low.

rubric.point: Push comments to viewers over persistent connections (SSE or WebSockets) instead of each client polling
Choose SSE vs WebSockets deliberately: viewers mostly receive, so SSE (one-way over HTTP) is enough, with comments posted via a normal POST
Fan out through pub/sub: a comment is published to a channel for that live video, and every server holding viewers of it forwards it
Route viewers of the same video to the same connection servers (consistent hashing on video ID) so each server subscribes to few channels
Hold millions of idle connections on a dedicated, horizontally scaled connection tier, separate from the comment-writing path
Persist comments durably in a write-optimised store (e.g. Cassandra) partitioned by video ID and ordered by time
Let late joiners and scroll-back fetch recent history with cursor-based pagination
Handle massively popular streams: sample, rate-limit or batch comments per viewer, since nobody can read 10,000 comments a second
State the trade-off: low delivery latency (about 1-2 seconds) with eventual consistency and best-effort ordering, not strict global order

functional: Viewers post comments on a live video
Viewers watching the live video see new comments appear in near real time
Viewers who join late, or scroll up, can see earlier comments
nonFunctional: New comments appear for other viewers within about 2 seconds

Eventual consistency and best-effort ordering are acceptable; comment writes must be durable
Highly available; a comment spike on one stream must not affect others

deepDives.title: Pushing comments: SSE vs WebSockets vs polling
deepDives.body: Polling every second from millions of viewers is wasteful and still laggy. Viewers mainly receive, so SSE is a good fit: one-way push over plain HTTP, with automatic reconnects, while posting a comment is an ordinary POST. WebSockets work too and suit a product that needs bidirectional traffic, but they are harder to run through proxies and load balancers.

deepDives.title: Fan out across servers
deepDives.body: A viewer's connection lives on one of thousands of realtime servers, but a comment is written through any comment server. Pub/sub bridges the gap: the writer publishes to the video's channel and every subscribed realtime server broadcasts to its local connections. If viewers were spread randomly, every server would subscribe to nearly every channel; routing by video ID with consistent hashing keeps each server's subscriptions small and cuts duplicate traffic.

deepDives.title: Storing comments and history
deepDives.body: Comments are append-heavy and read by video in time order, which fits a wide column store like Cassandra partitioned by video_id and ordered by created_at. A late joiner loads the latest page, and scrolling up uses a cursor (the last comment's timestamp and id) rather than offsets, which stay stable while new comments keep arriving.

deepDives.title: Very popular streams
deepDives.body: A stream with 5 million viewers might get thousands of comments a second, far more than anyone can read. We can batch pushes (send a group every 500 ms), sample down to a readable rate per viewer while prioritising friends' comments, and rate limit each author. Ordering is best effort: comments can arrive a little out of order across servers, which is acceptable for this product.

rubric.point: Ingest articles by crawling publishers' RSS/Atom feeds and sitemaps on a schedule, with polling frequency tuned per publisher
Offer push ingestion too (webhooks or WebSub/PubSubHubbub) so big publishers' stories appear within minutes
Decouple ingestion from processing with a queue, and extract and normalise each article (title, summary, image, publish time, category)
Deduplicate syndicated and near-identical articles by URL canonicalisation and content fingerprints (simhash/minhash)
Cluster articles about the same story so the feed shows one story with several sources
Precompute feeds per category and region and cache them, since most readers see the same top stories
Paginate the feed with a cursor so new articles arriving don't cause duplicates or gaps while scrolling
Rank by recency plus signals such as source authority, cluster size and popularity; personalise lightly for signed-in users
Link out to the publisher and store only metadata, thumbnails (served via CDN) and short snippets, not full articles

deepDives.title: Ingesting from 100,000 publishers
deepDives.body: Most publishers expose RSS or Atom feeds, so a crawler polls them. Polling all of them every minute is wasteful, so each publisher gets an interval based on how often it posts (every 2 minutes for a major outlet, hourly for a small blog), with conditional GETs (ETag) to skip unchanged feeds. For the biggest publishers, a webhook or WebSub push cuts latency to seconds. All discovered URLs go through a queue so parsing can scale separately from fetching.

deepDives.title: Deduplication and story clustering
deepDives.body: The same wire story is republished by dozens of outlets, and one site may expose an article under several URLs. Canonicalising URLs catches exact copies, and a simhash fingerprint of the text catches near identical ones. Different articles about the same event are then grouped into a cluster using text similarity or embeddings, so the feed shows one story with several sources instead of ten similar headlines.

deepDives.title: Serving a fast feed
deepDives.body: Hundreds of millions of readers mostly see the same top stories per category and region, so we precompute those ranked lists every minute or so and cache them in Redis. The feed request becomes a cache read, well under 200 ms. Pagination uses a cursor (last score and id) so that freshly inserted stories don't shift pages and cause duplicates while a reader scrolls. Light personalisation re-ranks the cached list with the user's followed topics.

deepDives.title: Ranking and freshness
deepDives.body: A story's score blends recency (decaying over hours), the authority of its sources, how many publishers cover it, and click popularity. We store only metadata, a short snippet and a thumbnail, then link out to the publisher's site, which keeps storage small and respects publishers' content.

Prioritise what to crawl: popular and watched products are re-checked often, the long tail rarely, using a priority queue
Crowdsource prices from a browser extension as users view pages, validated against trusted crawls
Store price history in a time-series friendly layout (product ID plus timestamp), only writing when the price changes
Model alerts as subscriptions with a target price; find the ones to fire efficiently by indexing on product and threshold
Detect price drops in a stream: price-change events go to a queue and a consumer checks matching subscriptions
Send notifications (email or push) through a separate notification service, with dedup so a user isn't alerted repeatedly for the same drop
Render the price history chart quickly by caching or pre-aggregating chart data per product
Size it: hundreds of millions of products, so full crawls every hour are impossible; budget crawl throughput per second

deepDives.title: Keeping prices fresh with a crawl budget
deepDives.body: Checking 500 million products hourly would mean ~140,000 fetches per second, far beyond what Amazon allows. So we prioritise: products with active alerts or lots of views are checked every hour or so, and the long tail maybe weekly. A priority queue keyed on next-check time drives the crawlers, and products whose price changes often are promoted. The official affiliate/product API is preferred where it covers the item, with scraping as a fallback.

deepDives.title: Crowdsourcing via a browser extension
deepDives.body: Users with the extension see Amazon prices anyway, so the extension can report them, giving fresh data on popular products for free. Because reports can be wrong or malicious, we only accept prices that are consistent across several users, or confirm a surprising drop with a targeted crawl before alerting.

deepDives.title: Storing price history
deepDives.body: Prices change rarely, so we write a PricePoint only when the price changes, which shrinks storage enormously. A time series layout keyed by (asin, timestamp), in Cassandra or TimescaleDB, makes 'give me this product's last year' one sequential read. Long ranges can be downsampled into daily rollups, and the rendered chart data is cached per product.

deepDives.title: Firing alerts efficiently
deepDives.body: Each price change event is processed by a consumer that queries subscriptions indexed by (asin, target_price) for all targets at or above the new price, so we never scan all 50 million alerts. Matches are sent to a notification service for email or push. We record last_notified_price so a user gets one alert per drop, not one on every crawl while the price stays low.

Use separate queues and worker pools per channel (push, email, SMS) so a slow provider doesn't block the others
Deliver through third-party providers: APNs/FCM for push, an email provider such as SES/SendGrid, and an SMS gateway such as Twilio
Respect user preferences and opt-outs per channel and category, plus quiet hours and legal unsubscribe rules
Retry failed sends with exponential backoff, and park permanent failures in a dead-letter queue
Avoid duplicate notifications: an idempotency key per notification, checked before sending, since queues deliver at least once
Rate limit per user and per provider to avoid spamming people and exceeding provider quotas
Prioritise urgent messages (OTPs, security alerts) over bulk marketing with priority queues
Store templates and render per locale, and keep device tokens and contact details up to date (remove invalid tokens)
Track delivery status per notification (sent, delivered, opened, failed) via provider callbacks for analytics

deepDives.title: Asynchronous, per-channel pipeline
deepDives.body: Sending synchronously would make every caller wait on slow providers. Instead the API writes to a queue and returns, and workers do the sending. Each channel gets its own queue and workers, so if the SMS provider slows down, emails and push still flow. Workers are stateless and scale on queue depth, which absorbs campaign peaks of a million messages per second.

deepDives.title: Reliability: retries and duplicates
deepDives.body: Providers fail transiently, so workers retry with exponential backoff and jitter, and move messages that keep failing (or fail permanently, like an invalid phone number) to a dead-letter queue. Queues deliver at least once, so a crash after sending but before acknowledging can resend. An idempotency key per notification and channel, recorded in Redis or the database when sent, lets workers skip ones already delivered, keeping duplicates rare.

deepDives.title: Preferences, rate limits and priority
deepDives.body: Before sending, the router checks the user's preferences and opt-outs per category and channel, respects quiet hours by delaying non-urgent messages, and applies a per-user frequency cap so nobody gets spammed. Provider quotas are also rate limited. Urgent messages like OTPs and security alerts use a high priority queue with reserved workers, so a bulk marketing campaign never delays a login code.

deepDives.title: Templates, contacts and tracking
deepDives.body: Senders reference a template plus parameters, and the router renders it in the user's locale, which keeps copy consistent and easy to change. Device tokens go stale when apps are uninstalled; when APNs or FCM report an invalid token we remove it. Provider callbacks and open tracking update each notification's status, feeding delivery analytics and debugging.

rubric.point: Don't write a database row per view: send view events into a log (Kafka) and count them in stream processors partitioned by video ID
Sliding windows come from time buckets: keep per-minute (or per-hour) counts, add the newest bucket and subtract the one that falls out of the window
Each shard keeps a local top K (a min-heap); a merge step combines the shard lists into the global top K
Hot videos can overwhelm one partition: combine counts locally before sending them on, or salt the key and sum the pieces
Queries read a precomputed top-K list per window from a cache, not by scanning counts at request time
Exact counting of every video is expensive; approximate structures (count-min sketch plus a heap of heavy hitters) trade a small error for tiny memory
Say how fresh results must be: a minute of lag is usually fine, which lets you batch and cache aggressively
Recover from crashes by checkpointing counter state together with the Kafka offset, then replaying from that offset
Avoid double counting: give each view event an ID and make processing idempotent / exactly-once so retries don't inflate counts
Long windows (month, all time) use coarser buckets (hourly/daily) and can be recomputed or reconciled by a batch job
Back-of-the-envelope: billions of views a day is roughly a million events per second at peak, far too many for synchronous writes

functional: Return the top K most-viewed videos for a window: last hour, last day, last month, all time
K is bounded (say up to 1,000) and results can be filtered to one window per call
Views are counted from the playback event stream the client already emits
nonFunctional: Ingest about 70 billion views a day, around 1 million view events per second at peak
Top-K queries return in under 100 ms
Results may lag by up to about a minute (eventual consistency, freshness over precision is fine within limits)
No view is counted twice after a crash or retry
Hundreds of millions of distinct videos, most with very few views (a long tail)

Each processor maintains a local top-K min-heap per window and publishes it every few seconds
A merger reads the per-shard lists, merges them into the global top K and writes the result to Redis
The query service simply reads the precomputed list for the requested window from the cache
Raw events are also landed in object storage for a nightly batch job that recomputes month and all-time counts

deepDives.title: Sliding windows with buckets
deepDives.body: Keeping every timestamp per video is impossible, so bucket counts: per-minute buckets for the hour window, hourly buckets for the day, daily buckets for the month. When a minute ends, add the newest bucket to the running hour total and subtract the bucket that has just fallen out of the window, so each window update is O(1) per video. All-time is a single running counter. The trade-off is granularity: the 'last hour' is really the last 60 whole minutes, which nobody minds. A Redis sorted set or the processor's local state holds the running totals.

deepDives.title: Merging per-shard top K
deepDives.body: Because each video lives on exactly one partition, a video's count is complete within its shard, so the global top K is guaranteed to be inside the union of each shard's local top K. Each shard keeps a min-heap of size K per window: when a video's count beats the heap minimum, it replaces it. A merger gathers N lists of K entries and takes the top K, which is cheap even for hundreds of shards. This only works because partitioning is by video ID; had we partitioned randomly, each shard would hold partial counts and local heaps could miss the true winners.

deepDives.title: Hot videos and throughput
deepDives.body: At a million events per second, writing to a database per view is out, so aggregation happens in memory. A viral video can still flood its single partition, so producers or an ingest tier run a combiner: they sum views per video for a second or two and send one (video_id, +n) message instead of n messages. If one video is still too hot, salt its key into several sub-keys and sum them at merge time. The cost of pre-aggregation is a couple of seconds of extra lag, which fits the freshness budget.

deepDives.title: Exactness, crashes and double counting
deepDives.body: Stream processors checkpoint their bucket state and the Kafka offset atomically (Flink does this with barriers), so after a crash they restore the snapshot and replay from the saved offset without counting anything twice: effectively exactly-once. Clients retrying a view send the same event_id, and a short-lived dedup set (or the ingest layer) drops duplicates. If we wanted to save memory we could track the long tail with a count-min sketch and keep only heavy hitters exactly; the sketch over-counts slightly, which is acceptable for a ranking but not for billing. The nightly batch job over raw events is the source of truth and reconciles any drift.

deepDives.title: Serving and freshness
deepDives.body: The top-K list for each window is small (K entries), so the merger writes it to Redis every few seconds and the read path is a single key lookup, easily under 100 ms at any read rate. Results are therefore up to about a minute stale, which should be agreed with the interviewer up front. Month and all-time windows change slowly, so they can be refreshed less often and backed by the batch recomputation, while the hour window gets the fastest refresh.

rubric.point: Drivers send GPS location updates every few seconds, so the location path is extremely write-heavy and belongs in memory, not a relational table
Find nearby drivers with a geospatial index: geohash, quadtree, H3 hexagons or Redis GEO commands
A driver must never be offered two rides at once: take a short lock/lease on the driver (e.g. Redis SET NX with a TTL) or a conditional write
Offers time out: if a driver declines or ignores the request for ~10 s, move on to the next-best driver, driven by a durable workflow
Put ride requests on a queue so surges at peak times are buffered rather than dropped
Shard the location index and matching by region/city; dense areas get more, smaller partitions
Rank candidates by ETA over the road network (routing service with traffic), not straight-line distance
Push offers to drivers and trip updates to riders over persistent connections or push notifications
Cut load by making the update frequency adaptive: less often when stationary or offline, more often near a pickup
Ride creation, acceptance and payment must be idempotent so client retries don't create duplicate rides or charges
Plan for failure: the location index is ephemeral and rebuilds from the next pings, while ride state lives in a durable, replicated store
Back-of-the-envelope: a few million online drivers updating every 5 s is roughly a million location writes per second

Riders request a ride and are matched with a nearby available driver
Drivers accept or decline ride offers and update their location and availability
Both sides see live trip status and the driver's position
nonFunctional: Matching completes within about 1 minute, with each offer answered or timed out in ~10 s
Strong consistency for assignment: a driver is never matched to two rides at once
About 5 million online drivers updating location every 5 s → roughly 1 million writes per second
Highly available during surges such as concerts or New Year's Eve (10× peak)
Location reads can be a few seconds stale

A location service ingests driver pings into an in-memory geospatial index (Redis GEO or an H3 cell map), sharded by city/region

deepDives.title: High-frequency location updates
deepDives.body: A million GPS writes per second would crush a relational database with index maintenance, and nobody needs yesterday's positions for matching. Keep only the latest position per driver in Redis using geohash-based GEO commands (GEOADD / GEOSEARCH), sharded by region so each shard handles one city's drivers. Old entries expire with a TTL so offline drivers vanish automatically. If trip history is needed, stream the pings to Kafka and on to cheap storage asynchronously. Adaptive intervals help too: a stationary or offline driver pings rarely, a driver approaching a pickup more often, which saves bandwidth and battery.

deepDives.title: Geospatial search choices
deepDives.body: A geohash or H3 index maps each location to a cell, so 'nearby' becomes a lookup of the rider's cell plus its neighbours, which suits constant updates. A quadtree adapts cell size to density (small cells downtown, large ones in the countryside) but is costlier to rebalance under a million updates per second. Whichever index is used, it only produces candidates by straight-line distance; the top few are then ranked by ETA from a routing service that knows the road network and traffic, because a driver across a river may be close but 20 minutes away.

deepDives.title: Never double-assign a driver
deepDives.body: Two matching workers may pick the same driver for two riders at the same moment. Before sending an offer, the worker takes a lock on the driver with Redis SET driver:{id} rideId NX EX 10; only one worker wins and the others move to their next candidate. The TTL equals the offer timeout, so a crashed worker or an unresponsive driver releases the lock on its own. When the driver accepts, the ride row is updated with a conditional write (status = offered AND driver_id = X) so a late acceptance of an expired offer is rejected. This keeps assignment strongly consistent without locking anything globally.

deepDives.title: Timeouts, retries and surges
deepDives.body: Each ride request is a small workflow: find candidates, offer to the best, wait ~10 s, and on a decline or timeout offer to the next driver, widening the search radius after a few misses. Running this in a durable workflow engine (Temporal, or a state machine persisted in the database) means a worker crash resumes the ride instead of losing it. Requests enter a queue partitioned by region, so a surge in one city builds a backlog there instead of dropping requests or starving other cities. Ride creation carries an idempotency key so a rider tapping twice, or a mobile retry, doesn't create two rides.

deepDives.title: Failure and recovery
deepDives.body: If a location shard dies, a replica takes over or it simply refills: every online driver pings again within 5 s, so the ephemeral index rebuilds itself almost immediately. Ride state is the part that must survive, so it lives in a replicated database with synchronous commits and automatic failover. Drivers' and riders' WebSocket connections can land on any connection server; if one fails, clients reconnect and resubscribe, and the latest ride status is re-read from the database so nothing depends on in-memory connection state.

rubric.point: Robinhood is a broker, not an exchange: orders are routed to an external exchange or market maker (typically via the FIX protocol), which does the matching
Live prices: consume the exchange's market data feed once, then fan out to clients over WebSockets or server-sent events
Scale fan-out with per-symbol pub/sub channels and connection servers that only subscribe to the symbols their clients watch
Clients don't need every tick: conflate or throttle updates to the latest price every few hundred milliseconds
Model orders as a state machine persisted before anything is sent: pending → submitted → partially filled / filled / cancelled / rejected
Use a client-generated order ID as an idempotency key so retries never place duplicate orders
Fills arrive asynchronously as execution reports; reconcile against the exchange's records to catch anything missed
Handle crashes between saving and sending an order: an outbox / write-ahead record plus recovery that asks the exchange about in-flight orders
Check and reserve buying power atomically when the order is placed so a user can't overspend with concurrent orders
Cancels race with fills: a cancel is only a request, and the exchange's answer (cancel ack or already filled) is final
Orders and positions need strong consistency: an ACID relational store, sharded by user
Back-of-the-envelope: tens of millions of users, ~10k symbols, bursts of price updates per second at market open

deepDives.title: Fanning out live prices
deepDives.body: The exchange feed is consumed once by the market data service; connecting millions of phones to it directly is impossible and costly. Each tick is published to a channel per symbol, and each connection server subscribes to the union of symbols its clients watch, so a server with 50k clients may only need a few hundred channels. Hot symbols (a meme stock at market open) are handled by the same design because each server receives a symbol's tick once, however many local clients want it. Phones can't render 50 ticks a second anyway, so servers conflate: they keep the latest price per symbol and push it every 200–500 ms, which caps bandwidth during bursts. Server-sent events are enough if the client never sends more than subscriptions; WebSockets make subscription changes simpler.

deepDives.title: Order lifecycle and idempotency
deepDives.body: An order is written as pending, with the client's clientOrderId under a unique constraint, before anything goes to the exchange. If the phone retries after a timeout, the insert hits the constraint and we return the existing order instead of creating a duplicate, so each tap is effectively exactly-once. The status then moves through submitted, partially filled, filled, cancelled or rejected purely in response to execution reports, and every transition is applied in a transaction that also updates filled quantity, positions and cash. Keeping the state machine explicit makes it easy to reject impossible transitions such as a fill after a final reject.

deepDives.title: Surviving crashes around the exchange
deepDives.body: The dangerous moment is between saving an order and knowing whether the exchange received it. Using an outbox, the order row and a 'to submit' record are written in one transaction; the gateway submits it and marks it sent, and it reuses the same client order ID so a resend after a crash is recognised by the exchange as a duplicate. On restart, the gateway finds orders that are in flight in an unknown state and queries the exchange for their status rather than guessing. Execution reports are handled idempotently by exchange execution ID, and a reconciliation job against the exchange's drop copy catches any mismatch before end of day.

deepDives.title: Buying power, cancels and races
deepDives.body: Placing a buy order reserves its maximum cost in the same transaction that inserts the order (UPDATE account SET reserved = reserved + x WHERE cash − reserved ≥ x), so two concurrent orders can't both spend the same cash; the hold is released or converted to a real debit as fills arrive. A cancel only marks the order pending cancel and sends a cancel request; the exchange may reply that it was already filled, and that answer wins, because the exchange is the source of truth. The client should show 'cancel requested' rather than 'cancelled' until the ack arrives, which avoids promising something we can't guarantee.

deepDives.title: Data model and scaling
deepDives.body: Orders, positions and cash need ACID transactions and strong consistency, so a relational database such as Postgres fits, sharded by user ID because almost every query and transaction is scoped to one user. Market data is the opposite: huge volume, disposable, and fine to lose a tick, so it stays in memory and pub/sub. Order volume is modest (thousands per second at market open), so the order path scales with a handful of shards; the price fan-out, with millions of connections, is where most servers go.

rubric.point: Resolve concurrent edits with operational transformation (OT) or CRDTs so every replica converges to the same text
Route all editors of a document to a single server that owns it (consistent hashing on document ID), so there is one place that orders operations
Clients keep persistent WebSocket connections for low-latency, two-way streaming of operations
The owner assigns each operation a revision number and appends it to a durable, versioned operation log
Periodically snapshot the document and compact the log so loading a document doesn't replay millions of operations
Cursors and presence are ephemeral: broadcast them to collaborators but don't persist them in the operation log
Offline edits queue locally and are rebased/transformed against missed operations when the client reconnects
Clients apply their own edits optimistically and keep them pending until the server acknowledges them with a revision
If the document server crashes, a new owner loads the latest snapshot plus log; operations must be durable before they are acked
Use a coordinator (ZooKeeper/etcd leases) for document ownership so two servers never both think they own a document (split brain)
Know the scale shape: billions of documents but only ~100 concurrent editors per document; cap editors and treat extra viewers as read-only

deepDives.title: OT versus CRDTs
deepDives.body: With operational transformation, a client sends an operation together with the revision it was based on; if other operations landed in between, the server transforms the incoming one against them (an insert at position 10 shifts to 13 if three characters were inserted earlier). OT is simple to reason about with a central server that decides the order, which is what Google Docs does. CRDTs such as Yjs or Automerge give every character a unique, ordered ID so replicas converge without a central authority, which suits peer-to-peer and offline-heavy apps, at the cost of extra metadata per character and tombstones for deletions. With a single owner per document, OT is the natural interview answer; mention CRDTs as the alternative and the trade-off.

deepDives.title: One owner per document
deepDives.body: Transformation needs a single, total order of operations, so every editor of a document must reach the same document server. The gateway uses consistent hashing on doc_id to pick the server, and the server holds a lease for that document in ZooKeeper or etcd so a network partition can't produce two owners (split brain). Because there are at most ~100 concurrent editors per document, one server comfortably handles a document; the platform scales by spreading billions of documents across many servers. Viewers beyond a cap receive the stream read-only, perhaps via a separate fan-out tier, so a viral document can't overload its owner.

deepDives.title: Operation log and snapshots
deepDives.body: The owner assigns each accepted operation the next revision number and appends it to an append-only operation log; only after that durable write does it ack the author and broadcast to others. The log gives version history for free and lets a lagging client catch up by asking for everything after its last revision. Replaying millions of operations to open a document would be slow, so a background worker writes a snapshot every few hundred operations and older operations can be compacted or moved to cold storage. Loading a document is then 'latest snapshot plus the short tail of the log'.

deepDives.title: Client behaviour: optimistic edits and offline
deepDives.body: Typing must feel instant, so the client applies its own edit locally straight away and sends it, keeping at most one operation in flight and buffering the rest until an ack with a revision arrives. Incoming remote operations are transformed against the client's pending ones so the local view stays correct. Offline editing is the same mechanism stretched out: edits queue locally, and on reconnect the client sends its base revision, receives the missed operations and rebases its queue on top of them. Long offline sessions can produce surprising merges, which is one reason CRDT-based editors are popular for offline-first apps.

deepDives.title: Failure recovery and presence
deepDives.body: If a document server crashes, its leases expire and the documents are reassigned to a new owner, which loads the latest snapshot plus the log tail and resumes from the last durable revision. Clients reconnect, send their last acknowledged revision and resend any unacknowledged operations, deduplicated by client_op_id so nothing is applied twice. Because operations are durable before they are acked, no acknowledged edit is lost. Cursors and presence are deliberately ephemeral: they are relayed in memory, rebuilt as clients reconnect, and losing them for a second is harmless.

Guard against crawler traps (infinite calendars, session IDs in URLs) with depth and per-domain page limits

Prioritise the frontier (importance, change frequency) and schedule recrawls for freshness

deepDives.title: Politeness and frontier partitioning
deepDives.body: A naive shared queue would let 100 workers hammer the same site at once. Instead, partition the frontier by a hash of the domain so all URLs for a host land in one partition consumed by one worker, which keeps a small per-domain queue and a next-allowed-fetch time. That worker reads robots.txt once (cached for a day), honours its crawl delay, and otherwise sends at most about one request per second per domain. A global rate limit in Redis per domain is an alternative when partitioning isn't possible. The cost is skew: a few huge domains create hot partitions, so very large sites can be spread over several sub-queues that still share one rate limit.

deepDives.title: Deduplication of URLs and content
deepDives.body: Before enqueueing a link, normalise it (lower-case host, strip fragments and tracking parameters, resolve relative paths, honour canonical tags), then check a seen-set. With tens of billions of URLs, a Bloom filter in memory answers 'definitely new' cheaply, with a small false-positive rate meaning we occasionally skip a new page, which is acceptable. Many different URLs serve the same page (mirrors, printer-friendly versions), so also hash the fetched content: an exact content hash catches identical pages and a SimHash fingerprint catches near duplicates before parsing and storage.

deepDives.title: Failures, retries and fault tolerance
deepDives.body: Fetches fail constantly (timeouts, 5xx, slow sites), so failed URLs are re-enqueued with exponential backoff (e.g. 30 s, 2 min, 10 min) and moved to a dead-letter queue after about five attempts. Workers are stateless: a worker takes a message, and if it crashes before deleting it, the queue's visibility timeout makes the message reappear for another worker, giving at-least-once delivery. Because a page might therefore be fetched twice, writes to S3 and the metadata store are idempotent (keyed by URL). Kafka consumers get the same effect by committing offsets only after processing.

deepDives.title: Traps, DNS and throughput
deepDives.body: Crawler traps such as infinite calendars or URLs that append session IDs can generate endless unique links, so enforce a maximum depth, a per-domain page budget and URL length limits, and down-rank patterns that keep producing near-duplicate content. At 23,000 pages per second, DNS becomes a surprising bottleneck; run local caching resolvers and cache results per domain for their TTL. Bandwidth, not CPU, is usually the limit: at ~500 KB per page that is roughly 10 GB/s across the fleet, so fetchers are spread over many machines and regions, and parsing runs on a separate pool that scales on its own queue depth.

deepDives.title: Storage and freshness
deepDives.body: Raw HTML goes to object storage such as S3 (petabytes, cheap and durable), while the URL table holds only metadata: status, last crawl time, content hash and the S3 key, in a key-value store like DynamoDB or Cassandra keyed by URL. For a one-off crawl that is enough; for a continuous crawl, the frontier becomes a priority queue where importance (PageRank-like scores) and observed change frequency decide how soon a page is recrawled, so news sites are revisited hourly and static pages monthly.

Aggregate per ad per minute and roll up to hourly and daily granularity for longer ranges
Don't count a click twice: attach a unique impression ID to each ad and deduplicate clicks on it
Protect against click fraud and spoofing: sign impression IDs and filter bots
Get exactly-once aggregation with stream checkpoints tied to Kafka offsets and a transactional or idempotent sink
Viral ads create hot partitions: salt the key (ad_id + random suffix) and sum the pieces later
Keep raw clicks in a data lake and run a periodic batch job that reconciles the streaming totals (billing must be right)
Handle late and out-of-order events with event-time windows and watermarks
Kafka retention lets you replay and reprocess after a bug or aggregator failure

Raw events are also sunk from Kafka to S3 (a data lake), where a periodic Spark batch job recomputes counts and reconciles them with the streaming results

deepDives.title: Click capture and redirect
deepDives.body: Letting the browser call the advertiser directly and report the click separately is unreliable (ad blockers, closed tabs), so the ad links to our endpoint. It verifies the impression ID, writes the click to Kafka and returns a 302 to the advertiser's URL, adding only a few milliseconds. Kafka is durable and absorbs peaks of 100k clicks per second, decoupling the redirect path from aggregation. If Kafka is briefly unavailable, the click service can buffer to local disk rather than fail the redirect.

deepDives.title: Stream aggregation and queries
deepDives.body: Flink consumes the topic partitioned by ad_id and counts clicks per ad in 1-minute tumbling windows keyed by event time, flushing each window's count to an OLAP store. Advertisers query ranges like 'last 30 days by day', so the OLAP store keeps minute rows and rolls them up to hourly and daily granularity, keeping queries under a second without scanning a billion raw clicks. Watermarks tell Flink when a minute is probably complete; events that arrive late within an allowed lateness update the window, and later stragglers are left to the batch reconciliation.

deepDives.title: Exactly-once counting, deduplication and fraud
deepDives.body: Two different problems cause wrong counts. Duplicate clicks (a user double-clicking, a retried request) are caught by the unique impression ID: the click service keeps recently seen IDs in Redis with a TTL and ignores repeats, so each impression is counted at most once. Signing the impression ID on the ad server stops people forging clicks for arbitrary ads, and bot or fraud filtering can run as a further stream step. Processing duplicates are handled by Flink's checkpoints, which store window state with Kafka offsets, plus a transactional or idempotent sink (upserts keyed by ad_id and minute), so a crash and restart gives exactly-once aggregates.

deepDives.title: Hot ads
deepDives.body: A Super Bowl ad can send a large share of all clicks to one ad_id, overloading its Kafka partition and Flink task. For ads known to be hot, the click service appends a random suffix (ad_id:0–N) to the partition key, spreading the load over N partitions; Flink aggregates each sub-key and a final step, or the OLAP query, sums them. Salting only the hot ads keeps normal ads simple, at the cost of a little extra coordination to know which ads are salted.

deepDives.title: Reconciliation and recovery
deepDives.body: Because advertisers are billed on these numbers, the streaming path is backed by a batch path in a lambda-style design. Raw clicks land in S3, and every hour or night a Spark batch job recomputes exact counts and reconciles them with the OLAP store, correcting any drift from late events or bugs. Kafka retention of several days means that after a bad deploy or an aggregator failure we can rewind consumer offsets and reprocess. Together these give fast approximate numbers within a minute and exact numbers for billing.
