deepDives.title: Why an inverted index, and how it is laid out
deepDives.body: Scanning billions of posts with LIKE '%word%' is impossible at 20k QPS, so we precompute an inverted index: keyword → list of post IDs. Because we only ever need the top of the list in one of two orders, we keep two posting lists per keyword, as Redis sorted sets scored by created_at and by like_count. A query then becomes a prefix read (ZREVRANGE with a cursor) instead of a sort at query time. Storing IDs only keeps the index small; post bodies come from a separate post cache. Elasticsearch could do the same job, but a purpose-built index makes the two sort orders and the like-update path explicit.

deepDives.title: Handling the like firehose
deepDives.body: Likes arrive at ~100k per second, ten times the post rate, and every like changes a score in every posting list that the post is in (one per word). Updating each on every like would melt the index. Instead a worker aggregates likes per post over a few seconds and only rewrites the like-sorted entries when the count crosses a threshold such as a power of two (1, 2, 4, 8 …). The index is then slightly stale, so the search service uses two-stage ranking: take the top few hundred candidates from the like-sorted list, refetch their fresh counts from the like counter and re-rank before returning the top 25. This trades a small amount of accuracy far down the list for an enormous cut in writes.

deepDives.title: Sharding and hot keywords
deepDives.body: We shard the index by keyword so each query touches one shard, rather than scattering to every shard as a document-partitioned index would. The downside is skew: a trending term like a sports final concentrates traffic and writes on one shard. Reads are handled by replicas of hot shards and by caching results at the CDN and in Redis with a TTL of 30–60 seconds, which is fine given the freshness target. Hot writes are smoothed by the Kafka buffer, and a very hot keyword can be split into sub-lists by time bucket.

deepDives.title: Multi-word queries
deepDives.body: For 'taylor swift' we intersect the two posting lists. Intersecting two lists of millions of IDs is expensive, so we only intersect the recent or top window (e.g. the first 10k entries of each) and page further if that yields too few results. Common pairs can be indexed directly as bigrams at ingestion time, turning a costly intersection into a single read at the price of a larger index. Rare combinations fall back to the slower intersection path.

deepDives.title: Keeping the index affordable
deepDives.body: An index over years of posts runs to terabytes, and keeping it all in memory is costly. Most searches hit recent posts and popular keywords, so we cap each in-memory posting list (say the newest and top 10k entries) and move the long tail and old postings to cold storage in S3, loaded on demand for rare deep-paging queries. Ingestion through Kafka also makes rebuilding the index from the post store possible if a shard is lost.

deepDives.title: Idempotency end to end
deepDives.body: Networks fail, so merchants retry and we must make retries harmless. The merchant sends an Idempotency-Key; we insert (merchant_id, key) with a unique constraint along with a hash of the request body. If the row exists and has a response, we return the stored response; if it is still in flight we return 409; if the body differs we reject the reuse. Internally we reuse the same idea when calling the processor: each attempt carries our payment_id as the processor's idempotency reference, so a retried authorisation cannot become two charges. Keys expire after about 24 hours. This gives effectively exactly-once charging on top of at-least-once networks.

deepDives.title: Payment state machine and unknown outcomes
deepDives.body: A PaymentIntent moves through created → processing → authorised → captured, with branches to failed, cancelled and refunded. Transitions are guarded with a conditional update (UPDATE … SET status='captured' WHERE id=? AND status='authorised'), so concurrent workers cannot apply the same step twice or skip a state. The hard case is a processor timeout: the charge may or may not have happened. We never mark it failed; it stays in processing, and a recovery worker retries with exponential backoff using the same reference, first querying the processor's status endpoint. Only a definitive answer moves it on, and anything still unresolved is caught by reconciliation.

deepDives.title: Double-entry ledger
deepDives.body: Balances are never stored as a single mutable number. Every money movement is a ledger transaction of at least two append-only entries whose debits and credits sum to zero: a capture debits the customer-funds account and credits the merchant's pending balance and our fee account. Balances are derived by summing entries (with periodic snapshots for speed). Mistakes are fixed with compensating entries, never edits, so the history is a complete audit trail. Writing the entries in the same ACID transaction as the status change means the ledger cannot drift from payment state.

deepDives.title: Reliable webhooks
deepDives.body: Writing the event to an outbox table in the same transaction as the state change guarantees we never change state without emitting an event. A relay pushes outbox rows to Kafka and a dispatcher POSTs them to merchants with at-least-once semantics: on a non-2xx or timeout it retries with exponential backoff for up to about three days, then marks the endpoint failing and lets the merchant replay from the dashboard. Each payload carries a unique event_id so merchants can dedupe, and a Signature header with an HMAC-SHA256 of a timestamp and the body, using the merchant's signing secret, so merchants can verify origin and reject replays. Per-merchant queues stop one slow endpoint from delaying everyone else.

deepDives.title: Reconciliation and PCI scope
deepDives.body: Even with careful retries, our records and the processor's can diverge (timeouts, processor bugs, chargebacks). A nightly job ingests settlement files and bank statements, matches them line by line against the ledger, and flags any discrepancy for automatic repair or manual review; this is the final safety net that makes the system correct. Separately, card numbers are the most sensitive data we hold, so they go directly from a hosted card field to a small tokenisation service with an HSM-encrypted vault. Only that service is in full PCI scope; the payments API, ledger and webhooks handle opaque tokens, which shrinks audit cost and blast radius.

Collectors validate, enforce per-tenant cardinality limits and write to Kafka, partitioned by series ID
Ingesters consume Kafka, hold recent data in memory and flush compressed, time-partitioned blocks to a time-series database; old blocks go to S3
A compaction job downsamples blocks into 1-minute and 1-hour rollups and enforces retention
A query service fans out to the in-memory ingesters and the stored blocks, merges results and caches them for Grafana-style dashboards
An alert evaluator runs rules every 15–30 s against the recent data, tracks pending/firing state and sends notifications through a deduping router

deepDives.title: Push vs pull, and buffering ingestion
deepDives.body: Pull (a Prometheus-style scraper) gives the server control over load and makes a dead host obvious, but at a million hosts the scrapers need their own service discovery and sharding, and short-lived batch jobs may vanish before being scraped. Push from agents scales more simply and works through NAT, so we push, batching and compressing every 10 s. Collectors write straight to Kafka rather than storage: the log absorbs spikes (a deploy restarts thousands of hosts at once), lets ingesters fall behind and catch up without dropping data, and lets us replay after a storage bug. Kafka also gives backpressure a place to live instead of pushing it back to every host.

deepDives.title: Time-series storage and compression
deepDives.body: A general-purpose database cannot absorb 10M inserts per second cheaply, so we use a time-series layout. Each series (metric name + labels) gets an ID; samples are appended to an in-memory head block per series and flushed every couple of hours as an immutable block. Timestamps arrive at regular intervals, so delta-of-delta encoding stores most in a bit or two, and values that change little compress well with XOR encoding (the Gorilla technique), giving ~1.4 bytes per point instead of 16. Series are sharded across ingesters by hashing the series ID with replication factor 3; hashing on the series rather than on time avoids every write landing on the 'current' shard. An inverted index from label to series IDs answers queries like service=checkout.

deepDives.title: Cardinality, downsampling and retention
deepDives.body: The real cost driver is not points but the number of distinct series. A label like user_id or request_id can create millions of series overnight and exhaust memory, so collectors enforce per-tenant and per-metric series limits and reject or drop offending labels, with a report back to the team. Old data is downsampled: raw 10 s data for 7 days, 1-minute rollups (min, max, sum, count) for 30 days and 1-hour rollups for a year. Keeping sum and count rather than just average lets rollups be combined correctly. Recent blocks sit on SSD, older ones in S3 as the cold tier, so a year of data stays affordable and long-range queries read far fewer points.

deepDives.title: Alerting that works when everything else is on fire
deepDives.body: Alerting is the part that must not fail, so the evaluator is a separate service with its own replicas reading from the ingesters' recent data, not from the dashboard query path. Rules are evaluated every 15–30 s; a rule must hold for a 'for' duration (say 2 minutes) before firing, which prevents flapping on a single noisy sample. Firing alerts go to a router that groups related alerts, dedupes across evaluator replicas and routes by severity to PagerDuty, Slack or email. Absence of data is itself an alert (a host that stops reporting is often the real incident), and a dead man's switch — a heartbeat alert that always fires and is watched by an external system — tells us if the monitoring pipeline itself has gone silent.

deepDives.title: Fast dashboards
deepDives.body: Popular dashboards are opened by dozens of engineers during an incident, each refreshing every 10 s. The query service splits requests into aligned time chunks and caches results per chunk, so only the newest chunk is recomputed on refresh. Long ranges are automatically served from rollups rather than raw data, and very expensive panels can be pre-aggregated as recording rules that are computed continuously at ingest. Per-query limits on series and points protect the storage layer from one accidental query that selects everything.

deepDives.title: Matchmaking
deepDives.body: Players waiting for a given time control are held in a Redis sorted set scored by rating. A matcher per pool repeatedly takes the longest-waiting player and looks for someone within a rating band that starts at ±50 and widens every few seconds, trading match quality for wait time. Removing both players and creating the game must be atomic, otherwise two matchers can pair the same person into two games; a Lua script that ZREMs both entries and only succeeds if both were present, or a single matcher process per pool partition, avoids this. Clients are told of the match over their WebSocket, and a player who has disconnected is dropped from the queue on heartbeat timeout.

deepDives.title: Authoritative game server and move ordering
deepDives.body: Each live game is owned by exactly one game server, chosen by consistent hashing on game_id, so there is a single writer and no distributed locking on the hot path. Every move carries the move number the client thinks it is playing; the server rejects a move if it is out of turn, the number doesn't match (a duplicate retry or a race) or it is illegal according to the rules engine. Accepted moves are appended with their number, so retries are idempotent. The server then pushes the move and updated clocks to the opponent's gateway via pub/sub; gateways stay stateless and only hold connections.

deepDives.title: Fair clocks
deepDives.body: The client's clock is only a display; the server's clock is the truth. The server stores each side's remaining time and the timestamp of the last move. When a move arrives it deducts the elapsed time from the mover, adds the increment and records the new timestamp. To avoid penalising players with slow connections, the client reports how long the move took locally and the server credits back measured network lag up to a small cap (lag compensation). For timeouts the owner schedules a timer for the moment the side to move would flag, so a player who simply stops moving still loses on time without any message arriving.

deepDives.title: Surviving disconnects and crashes
deepDives.body: If a player's connection drops, they reconnect to any gateway, which looks up the game and fetches its state (FEN, move list, clocks) to resync the board; their clock keeps running meanwhile, as in real chess. If a game server crashes, its games must not be lost: every accepted move is written to Redis with replication and appended to a durable log before being acknowledged. Another server picks up the game by consistent hashing, rehydrates it from that state and carries on. When the game ends the full PGN is archived to a durable store such as Cassandra or DynamoDB and the in-memory copy expires.

deepDives.title: Ratings, spectators and cheating
deepDives.body: When a game ends the owner emits a GameEnded event. A rating service consumes it and updates both players with Glicko-2 (or Elo) in a single transaction keyed on game_id, so a redelivered event is ignored. Spectators of a top game can number in the hundreds of thousands, so moves are broadcast through a pub/sub fan-out tier separate from the players' path, optionally with a short delay to stop live assistance. Cheat detection compares finished games with Stockfish evaluations and timing patterns in offline batch jobs, keeping expensive analysis away from move latency.

GPU inference is the scarce, expensive resource: a separate inference tier with a queue in front so bursts wait rather than overload the GPUs
Maximise GPU throughput with continuous (in-flight) batching of many requests and a KV cache for tokens already processed

Reuse prompt/prefix caching for shared system prompts and ongoing conversations, routing a conversation back to the same replica for cache hits
Rate limit and apply quotas per user and tier (tokens per minute), with priority classes for paid users when capacity is short
Autoscale GPU capacity on queue depth and tokens/s, knowing GPUs are slow to start and scarce, and shed or degrade load (smaller model) instead of failing
Handle dropped streams: persist the reply as it is generated so a reconnecting client can resume, and allow the user to stop generation to free GPU
Store conversations in a horizontally scalable store partitioned by user or conversation ID (e.g. Cassandra/DynamoDB)
Safety/moderation checks on input and output, run in parallel or on the stream so they add little latency
Estimate cost and load in tokens: requests per second × tokens per reply ÷ tokens/s per GPU gives the fleet size

deepDives.title: Streaming tokens
deepDives.body: A long reply can take 20–30 seconds to generate, so waiting for the whole thing would feel broken. We stream with server-sent events: a plain HTTP response that stays open and carries one small event per token or chunk, which works through proxies and suits one-way server → client traffic (WebSockets are fine too). Time to first token is dominated by queueing and the prompt 'prefill' step, so that is what we optimise and measure. Gateways must be tuned for many long-lived connections, and the stream is relayed from the model server through the chat service so the chat service can also persist it.

deepDives.title: Getting the most out of GPUs
deepDives.body: At ~10M tokens per second and perhaps a few thousand tokens per second per GPU for a large model with batching, the fleet runs to thousands of GPUs, so utilisation is everything. Generating one token for one request barely uses a GPU; batching many requests together multiplies throughput. Continuous batching adds and removes sequences from the running batch at each step instead of waiting for a whole batch to finish, so short replies don't wait on long ones. Each sequence keeps a KV cache of attention state for tokens already processed, and paged memory management lets many sequences share GPU memory without fragmentation. The trade-off is latency against throughput: bigger batches mean more tokens per GPU but slower tokens per user.

deepDives.title: Conversation history and the context window
deepDives.body: The model is stateless, so every turn we send the relevant history as part of the prompt. Messages are stored in Cassandra/DynamoDB partitioned by conversation ID (with a per-user index for the sidebar), with parent IDs so regenerated branches form a tree. Long conversations exceed the context window and make every turn more expensive, so we keep the most recent turns verbatim and replace older ones with a running summary, or retrieve only relevant earlier messages. Because the prompt for turn n+1 starts with the prompt for turn n, routing the conversation back to a replica that still holds that prefix in its KV cache (prefix caching) skips most of the prefill work.

deepDives.title: Capacity, fairness and overload
deepDives.body: GPUs cannot be spun up in seconds like web servers and may not be available at all during a spike, so we plan capacity for the daily peak and autoscale on queue depth and tokens per second within that envelope. Requests wait in a priority queue in front of the model servers: paid tiers and interactive chats ahead of free-tier and batch traffic. Per-user rate limits in tokens per minute stop one heavy user from starving others. When the queue grows beyond a latency budget we degrade rather than fail: route free users to a smaller, cheaper model, cap max output tokens, or show a 'at capacity' message, shedding load at the edge before it consumes GPU time.

deepDives.title: Dropped connections, stopping and safety
deepDives.body: Mobile connections drop mid-stream, so tokens are appended to the message record (in Redis, flushed to the conversation store on completion) as they arrive; a reconnecting client asks to resume from its last offset and gets the rest, and generation continues on the GPU regardless. When a user presses stop, the chat service cancels the inference request so the model server evicts the sequence from the batch and frees GPU time; the partial reply is saved with status stopped. Moderation classifiers check the user's input before inference and scan the output stream in chunks in parallel, cutting the stream if needed, so safety adds little to latency.

rubric.point: Never oversell: decrement stock atomically, e.g. a Redis DECR/Lua script or a conditional UPDATE … WHERE stock > 0, rather than read-then-write
Put a virtual waiting room / queue in front of checkout, admitting users at the rate the backend can handle with signed admission tokens
Serve the static product page and countdown from a CDN, so the spike of page loads never hits the origin
Reserve stock with a short hold (e.g. 10 minutes) and release it back if payment isn't completed in time
Hot key: a single stock counter is a hotspot, so shard the inventory into buckets across keys/nodes and keep it in memory
Process orders asynchronously: after winning a reservation, enqueue the order (Kafka/SQS) and let workers create orders and take payment at a steady rate
Keep the counter and the durable order database consistent: the order DB is the source of truth and a reconciliation job fixes drift after failures
Stop bots and abuse: CAPTCHA/proof of work, per-user and per-IP limits, one purchase per account
Idempotent purchase requests so impatient refreshes and retries don't create duplicate orders or double charges
Pre-scale and pre-warm for a known start time (instances, caches, connection pools) and load test beforehand, rather than relying on reactive autoscaling
Fail fast and shed load once stock is gone: a sold-out flag at the edge rejects further requests cheaply

Requests pass a bot filter (CAPTCHA, per-IP and per-account rate limits) and then a virtual waiting room that admits users at a controlled rate with signed admission tokens
The reservation service checks the token and per-user limit, then atomically decrements stock in Redis with a Lua script over sharded counter buckets and records a reservation with a TTL

A sweeper releases expired reservations back into the counter; a reconciliation job compares Redis with the database

deepDives.title: Absorbing the spike before it reaches the backend
deepDives.body: Most traffic is people refreshing the page, so the page and countdown are fully static on the CDN and the only dynamic bit is a tiny status JSON cached for a second at the edge. Buy attempts then go into a virtual waiting room: each user gets a queue position, and a gatekeeper admits users at the rate the reservation service can handle (say 20k per second), handing out short-lived signed admission tokens that the backend verifies without a lookup. This turns a million-request spike into a steady, controlled flow and makes fairness explicit; a random lottery among everyone who joined in the first minute is an alternative that removes the incentive to hammer refresh. Because the start time is known, instances, caches and connection pools are pre-scaled and pre-warmed and the whole path is load tested in advance; reactive autoscaling would be minutes too late.

deepDives.title: Atomic stock decrement without a hot key
deepDives.body: Read-then-write ('if stock > 0 then stock − 1') oversells under concurrency, so the decrement must be atomic: a Redis Lua script that checks and decrements in one step, or UPDATE sale SET stock = stock − 1 WHERE id = ? AND stock > 0 in a database. A single counter for a hugely popular item becomes a hot key that one Redis node must serialise, so we split the stock into, say, 20 buckets of 500 units on different shards and send each request to a random bucket, trying another if it is empty. When every bucket is empty we set a sold-out flag at the edge so further requests are rejected instantly and cheaply without touching Redis at all.

deepDives.title: Reservations and asynchronous orders
deepDives.body: Winning a unit creates a reservation with a 10-minute hold rather than a full order; the reservation request only has to touch Redis, so it is fast. The reservation is then enqueued to Kafka and order workers create the order row and call the payment provider at a steady rate the database can sustain, while the client polls or is pushed the status. If the user doesn't pay before expiry, or payment fails, a sweeper marks the reservation released and increments the counter so the unit returns to sale. This separates the burst-sensitive 'who gets a unit' decision from the slower, heavier order and payment work.

deepDives.title: Keeping Redis and the database consistent
deepDives.body: Redis is fast but can lose recent writes on failover, so it is a gate, not the record. The relational order database is the source of truth: each reservation is also written durably (in the same Lua step to a Redis stream consumed into the database, or via an outbox) and has a unique constraint on (sale_id, user_id) to enforce one purchase per account. A reconciliation job continually compares the counter with total stock minus held and paid reservations in the database and corrects drift. If in doubt, err towards undercounting stock: selling out a few units early is far cheaper than overselling and cancelling orders.

deepDives.title: Bots, retries and fairness
deepDives.body: Scalpers will script thousands of requests, so the waiting room requires a CAPTCHA or proof-of-work challenge to join, rate limits per IP and per account, and one reservation per user enforced both in the Lua script and by the database constraint. Real users mash refresh and retry on timeouts, so reserve and order calls carry an idempotency key: a retry returns the existing reservation or order rather than creating a duplicate or charging twice. Fraud checks on payment run in the order workers, off the hot path.
